subject: Government
title: The Civil Service and Public Administration
outline: Meaning of civil service and public service
Structure and hierarchy of the civil service
The Civil Service Commission and recruitment
Problems of the Nigerian civil service and reforms

modules.title: Nature, Structure and Features
modules.html:
1. Meaning

The civil service is the body of permanent, paid officials employed in the civil capacity of the state to advise on and implement government policy in ministries, departments and extra-ministerial agencies. The wider public service includes the civil service plus the police, armed forces, judiciary staff, public corporations, universities and local government employees.

2. Structure of a Ministry

LevelOfficerRole
Political headMinister / CommissionerPolicy direction and political responsibility
Administrative headPermanent Secretary / Director-GeneralChief adviser and accounting officer of the ministry
DirectorateDirectors and Deputy DirectorsHead departments and divisions
MiddleAssistant Directors, Chief and Principal OfficersBranches and sections
JuniorExecutive, clerical and support staffRoutine implementation

The service is grouped into classes: administrative, professional, executive, clerical and manipulative/auxiliary.

3. Features

  1. Permanence — officials remain when governments change.
  2. Neutrality — they serve any government of the day without partisanship.
  3. Anonymity — they act in the minister's name; the minister answers publicly.
  4. Impartiality — decisions follow rules, not personal or ethnic favour.
  5. Hierarchy — clear chain of command and channels of communication.
  6. Expertise and professionalism — recruitment by merit and competitive examination.
  7. Official secrecy — bound by the Official Secrets Act and oath.

4. Weber's Bureaucracy

Max Weber's ideal type of bureaucracy features hierarchy of offices, division of labour by specialisation, written rules and records, impersonality, recruitment and promotion by merit, and a career structure with fixed salaries. It maximises efficiency but risks red tape, rigidity and goal displacement, where rules become ends in themselves.

examples.q: A ministry is criticised in the National Assembly for a failed contract. Who answers and why?
examples.a: The Minister answers, under the doctrine of ministerial responsibility, because civil servants act anonymously in his name. Internally the Permanent Secretary, as accounting officer, bears responsibility for financial regularity and may be queried, disciplined or invited by the Public Accounts Committee, but publicly and politically the minister carries the blame.

examples.q: Why must the civil service be politically neutral?
examples.a: Because governments change but administration must continue. Neutrality ensures continuity of policy implementation, protects officials from dismissal on partisan grounds, guarantees that the incoming government inherits trustworthy advisers, and preserves public confidence that state resources are not used for party advantage.

modules.title: Functions, Commissions, Problems and Reform
modules.html:
1. Functions of the Civil Service

  1. Advising ministers on policy formulation.
  2. Implementing and administering approved policies and laws.
  3. Providing continuity and institutional memory.
  4. Delegated legislation: drafting rules and regulations.
  5. Quasi-judicial functions through tribunals and disciplinary panels.
  6. Collection of revenue and management of public finance.
  7. Delivery of public services and record keeping.
  8. Representing government in negotiations and international meetings.

2. The Federal Civil Service Commission

Established under section 153 of the 1999 Constitution, it appoints, promotes, transfers and disciplines civil servants (other than those in offices reserved to other bodies), insulating recruitment from political interference and applying the federal character principle.

3. Problems of the Nigerian Civil Service

ProblemEffect
Corruption and briberyInflated contracts, ghost workers, loss of revenue
Red tape and excessive procedureDelay in service delivery
Political interferenceErosion of neutrality and merit
Poor remuneration and welfareLow morale, brain drain, moonlighting
Overstaffing at junior levels, shortage of specialistsHigh wage bill, weak technical capacity
Nepotism and quota abuseMediocre appointments
Obsolete equipment and poor recordsInefficiency and lost files

4. Reform Efforts

  • Udoji Commission (1972–1974) — unified grading and salary structure, management by objectives.
  • Dotun Phillips Panel (1985) and the 1988 Civil Service Reorganisation Decree — made ministers chief executives and professionalised ministries; largely reversed in 1995 on the Ayida Panel's advice.
  • Ayida Review Panel (1994–1995) — restored the office of Permanent Secretary and the pool system.
  • Modern measures: monetisation of benefits, IPPIS payroll and BVN verification to remove ghost workers, e-governance, due process/BPP procurement reform, treasury single account, SERVICOM service charters, and performance-based promotion.

examples.q: Evaluate the impact of the 1988 civil service reform.
examples.a: It made the Minister both chief executive and accounting officer, abolished the pool system so that officers made careers within one ministry, and created professionalised directorates. Intended benefits were specialisation and clearer responsibility. In practice it politicised administration, eroded the neutrality and anonymity of career officers, weakened financial control and blurred the adviser–decider distinction, so the Ayida Panel recommended restoration of the Permanent Secretary system in 1995.

examples.q: How does the IPPIS reduce payroll fraud?
examples.a: The Integrated Personnel and Payroll Information System centralises staff records and pays salaries directly from a single database linked to Bank Verification Numbers. Duplicate and fictitious 'ghost workers' cannot survive biometric verification, and ministries lose the discretion to inflate nominal rolls, thereby cutting recurrent expenditure and improving transparency.

quiz.q: The administrative head of a Nigerian federal ministry is the:
quiz.solution: The Permanent Secretary is the career head and accounting officer of the ministry.

quiz.q: Civil servants remain in office when governments change because of:
The doctrine that a minister answers publicly for his ministry is:
Recruitment into the federal civil service is handled by the:
quiz.solution: Section 153 establishes the Commission to appoint, promote and discipline officers.
The Udoji Public Service Review Commission reported in 1974, introducing a unified grading structure.

quiz.q: Excessive adherence to rules and procedures is called:
quiz.solution: Red tape is bureaucratic delay caused by procedural rigidity.
The ideal type stresses hierarchy, written rules, impersonality and merit recruitment.

quiz.q: Which is NOT part of the civil service proper?
quiz.solution: Soldiers belong to the wider public service but not the civil service, which is civil in character.

quiz.q: The 1988 reform made the chief executive of a ministry the:
quiz.solution: The reform designated the Minister as chief executive and accounting officer.

options: Restoration of the Permanent Secretary system
quiz.solution: It reversed key 1988 changes and restored the traditional career structure.

quiz.q: Payment of salaries through a central biometric database is achieved by:
quiz.solution: IPPIS centralises personnel and payroll data to eliminate ghost workers.

quiz.q: Anonymity of civil servants means they:
options: Work without public credit or blame
quiz.solution: They act in the minister's name and are shielded from public accountability.

quiz.q: Which class of the civil service handles routine record keeping?
quiz.solution: The clerical class performs routine documentation and record duties.

quiz.q: Drafting of subsidiary rules under an Act is:
quiz.solution: Officials make regulations under powers delegated by the legislature.

quiz.q: A key cause of low morale in the Nigerian civil service is:
quiz.solution: Inadequate pay and welfare drive brain drain and corruption.
SERVICOM sets service charters and standards for public agencies.
